case_name: Case 1 — Reserve Coverage Test: Full Backing Verification (ART)

inputs.token_type: asset-referenced token (ART), Regulation (EU) 2023/1114, Title IV, Chapter 1
inputs.token_supply: 1,000,000 ART units outstanding, each redeemable at par €1.00
inputs.reserve_asset_A: €560,000.00 in cash deposits with a credit institution (regulated, EEA)
inputs.reserve_asset_C: €60,000.00 in high-quality liquid corporate bonds (EU/EEA, investment-grade), mark-to-market
inputs.regulatory_requirement: 100% (1:1) full backing — reserve must equal or exceed the amount of tokens in circulation

computation: Step 1: Aggregate token redemption value at par
Coverage ratio = total reserve value ÷ aggregate token value
Reserve coverage is ADEQUATE — the issuer holds assets exceeding the full redemption value of outstanding tokens by €50,000.00 (5.00 percentage points).

result.verdict: ADEQUATE — reserve covers the full redemption obligation; issuer complies with the full-backing requirement

article_basis: Regulation (EU) 2023/1114, Article 48(1) — asset-referenced token issuers must hold reserve assets in the amount of the tokens in circulation; full backing is required (100% of the value of the tokens). Article 48(2) specifies the types of eligible reserve assets (cash, units in a UCITS/pension funds/undertakings for collective investment in transferable securities, or other assets with equivalent credit quality and liquidity). The coverage test compares the aggregate fair value of reserve assets to the aggregate redemption value of outstanding tokens.
tail_convention: Coverage ratio: higher is better (more reserve relative to token value = more adequate). The adverse tail for coverage is the LOW tail — a coverage ratio below 100% indicates reserve insufficiency. This test correctly examines adequacy by checking whether coverage ≥ 100% (the entire distribution is above the threshold in this case, so no adverse-tail concern arises).
weakest_point: The exact regulatory test is 100% full backing (reserve ≥ tokens in circulation). The computation is simple arithmetic and internally consistent. The weakest point is whether the characterisation of reserve assets B and C as eligible under Article 48(2) is fully precise — Article 48 limits eligible reserves to cash, certain funds, and other assets meeting specified quality/liquidity criteria — and I have not verified each asset class against the exact eligibility criteria in the text. The coverage arithmetic itself is exact and the pass/fail is unambiguous.

case_name: Case 2 — Own-Funds Requirement Computation for an ART Issuer

inputs.average_reserve_assets_30day: €1,050,000.00 (30-calendar-day average, weighted by the number of business days, of the value of covered reserve assets held)
inputs.own_funds_available: €30,000.00 (eligible own funds as defined under MiCA / CRR), consisting of:
inputs.equity_capital_in_issuer: €25,000.00 common ordinary share capital (fully paid up)
inputs.goodwill_intangible: €1,000.00 — excluded from eligible own funds (not allowed per standard regulatory deduction)
inputs.risk_weighted_exposure_note: ART own-funds test under Article 35 is a FIXED-PERCENTAGE test on average reserve assets, not a risk-weighted exposure-based test — the computation uses average reserve assets directly

computation: Step 1: Identify the own-funds requirement formula per Article 35
Article 35(1): ART issuers must hold own funds equal to at least 2% of the average amount
of reserve assets held during the preceding 30 calendar days.
Article 35 also sets an ABSOLUTE MINIMUM: €150,000 (the 'fixed minimum').
The issuer's own-funds must satisfy BOTH: ≥ 2% × average reserve AND ≥ €150,000.
(Note: Article 35 distinguishes different thresholds for different ART types; I am using
the single threshold of 2% + €150,000 minimum as the general case — I am reasonably
confident this is the correct general threshold for non-shortage ART but flag it as a
Step 3: Compare to the absolute minimum
Gross own funds = equity capital + retained earnings = €25,000.00 + €4,000.00 = €29,000.00
(Note: goodwill treated as ineligible per standard Basel/Central Bank own-funds
treatment — MiCA own-funds requirements typically follow the CRR treatment with
Step 5: Compare eligible own funds to binding requirement
INADEQUATE — the issuer holds €28,000.00 of eligible own funds against a requirement of
€150,000.00 (driven by the absolute minimum, not the percentage test).
The shortfall of €122,000.00 must be remedied by increasing own funds to at least
€150,000.00, or by reducing the average reserve assets so the percentage test binds
at a lower level — but the absolute minimum of €150,000 applies regardless.

result.verdict: INADEQUATE — own funds short by €122,000.00; binding constraint is the €150,000 minimum, not the 2% percentage test

article_basis: Regulation (EU) 2023/1114, Article 35 — own funds requirement for asset-referenced token issuers. Article 35(1) sets a percentage-of-average-reserve requirement (the '2%' rate) and an absolute minimum euro amount. The specific percentage (2%) and minimum (€150,000) I have used are the values I am most confident about for the general ART case, but I am not 100% certain whether the Commission Delegated Regulation or the EBA RTS have modified these figures, or whether different ART categories (e.g. basket-referenced, single-asset-referenced) have different thresholds. I have named the parameters explicitly but I AM NOT CERTAIN the current regulatory values are exactly 2% / €150,000 — they are plausible and consistent with my recollection of the framework, but the prompt's hard rule forbids invented percentages; I am treating them as best-known values with that caveat.
tail_convention: Own-funds adequacy: higher own funds relative to the requirement is the favorable tail; the adverse tail is the LOW end — an issuer with own funds BELOW the requirement. This case correctly examines the adverse tail (own funds shortfall) and correctly applies max(percentage_requirement, absolute_minimum) as the binding test.
weakest_point: The single most uncertain detail is whether the current Article 35 percentage is exactly 2% and the minimum exactly €150,000. These figures are plausible but could be modified by delegated acts or differ by ART category. I have not verified them against the precise current text of the Regulation as amended. The computation mechanics (percentage × average, max with minimum, deduction of goodwill) are correct structural logic, but the input constants carry uncertainty.

case_name: Case 3 — Stressed Coverage Test: Reserve Asset Haircuts and Retest

inputs.token_type: asset-referenced token (ART), Regulation (EU) 2023/1114, Article 48 (reserve coverage) and Article 49 (stress testing / early warning indicators)
inputs.pre_stress_token_supply: 1,000,000 ART units outstanding, par €1.00 each → €1,000,000.00 redemption value

pre_stress_reserve_breakdown.cash: €560,000.00 (haircut: 0% — cash held at par; nominal value retained)

inputs.stress_scenario: adverse stress: broad market downturn, credit spread widening, liquidity freeze — applied haircuts are COUNTERPARTY/ASSET haircuts reducing the fair value of reserve assets held

computation: Step 1: Apply stress haircuts to each reserve asset class

INADEQUATE under stress — the reserve coverage falls to 99.50%, below the 100% full-backing requirement. The issuer would need to either replenish the reserve (by adding €5,000.00 or more in eligible assets), reduce the amount of tokens in circulation, or adjust the reserve asset composition to withstand the stress scenario.
Step 6: Note on early warning / remediation
Article 49 and related provisions require ART issuers to conduct stress testing and to
trigger early warning indicators if coverage approaches or falls below 100%. A stressed
coverage of 99.50% would trigger such remediation obligations.

result.verdict: INADEQUATE UNDER STRESS — coverage falls below 100%; issuer must remedy the €5,000.00 shortfall

article_basis: Regulation (EU) 2023/1114, Article 48 (reserve assets and full backing, including stress testing requirements), Article 49 (obligations to maintain adequate reserves, early warning indicators, and stress testing). The stress test examines how the reserve coverage ratio behaves when reserve assets are marked down under an adverse scenario. Article 48(3)-(5) addresses the maintenance of adequate reserves under normal and stressed conditions.
tail_convention: Coverage ratio: higher is better; the adverse tail is the LOW tail (coverage below 100%). Under stress, the reserve assets DECREASE — this directly compresses coverage toward (and in this case below) the 100% threshold. The test correctly examines the stress scenario because stress REDUCES coverage, and the adverse condition (coverage < 100%) occurs in the downward direction. The stress test examines the correct (adverse) tail.
weakest_point: The stress haircuts (10% on government bonds, 20% on corporate bonds) are illustrative — I have chosen them as plausible stress severities but I have not sourced them from an official MiCA stress scenario or regulatory standard. The actual Article 49 stress testing framework would be specified by the EBA and the Commission, and the severity of haircuts is not something I can state with certainty. The arithmetic under the chosen haircuts is exact; the haircut values themselves are the uncertainty.

case_name: Case 4 — Redemption-at-Par Obligation: Cash-Flow Math at Par Redemption

inputs.token_type: asset-referenced token (ART), fully backed at 105% pre-stress (from Case 1 scenario)
inputs.token_holders_redeeming: 400,000 ART units tendered for redemption in a single redemption window
inputs.redemption_price: €1.00 per token (AT PAR — exactly the nominal value, no premium, no discount)
inputs.reserve_asset_sales_for_redemption: issuer must liquidate €400,000.00 of reserve assets to fund redemptions — assume the issuer sells the required amount from the government bond portfolio at the mark-to-market value (no additional selling cost in this simple case)

computation: Step 1: Compute the redemption payment obligation
Step 2: Verify the issuer's ability to pay at par
The redemption payment of €400,000.00 is less than the cash on hand.
Even without selling any bonds, the issuer can pay the full €400,000.00 from existing cash.
(Additional reserve assets — the government bonds and corporate bonds — provide a
secondary source of liquidity if needed.)
Step 3: Effect on reserve adequacy post-redemption
Tokens in circulation after redemption = 1,000,000 − 400,000 = 600,000 ART
Reserve composition after redemption (assuming bonds sold and cash paid out):
Cash:                 €560,000.00 (unchanged — cash was used and replenished via bond sale)
Coverage INCREASED from 105.00% to 108.33% because the issuer held reserve assets
exceeding the par value of redeemed tokens — the excess reserve (€50,000.00 from Case 1)
is now spread across fewer tokens, and the cash buffer remained intact.
Redemption paid in full at par:  €400,000.00  →  CORRECT
No shortfall:  the issuer honoured all redemption requests at par without any haircut, delay, or partial payment.

result.verdict: REDEMPTION HONOURED AT PAR — all 400,000 tokens redeemed at €1.00 each; reserve coverage improved to 108.33%; no shortfall, no haircut, no breach

article_basis: Regulation (EU) 2023/1114, Article 48 (reserve assets), Article 46 (redemption at par — the issuer must redeem ART at the par value at the time of the request; no haircutting, no delay, no partial payment — the right of holders to redeem at par is central to the stablecoin framework). Article 47 addresses the process of redemption (including timelines and the obligation to redeem tokens at par without any deduction).
tail_convention: Redemption at par: the adverse outcome is a failure to redeem at full par (haircut, delay, partial payment). The favorable outcome is full, prompt redemption at €1.00/token. This case correctly examines the redemption obligation math and confirms the issuer can meet the par obligation — the favorable tail is satisfied. No adverse tail action occurs.
weakest_point: The redemption math is simple arithmetic (400,000 × €1.00 = €400,000.00) and internally consistent. The weakest point is the assumption about reserve asset liquidity — I assumed the government bonds could be sold at par (mark-to-market) without a discount, transaction cost, or market impact. In reality, selling €400,000.00 of bonds in stressed conditions could require a haircut or delay, which would compress the post-redemption coverage. The computation assumes perfect liquidity for the bond sale, which is a simplification. Also, the characterisation of the post-redemption reserve composition (cash unchanged because bond sale proceeds replenish cash) is consistent but could be constructed differently.
